lines: Your money is only worth what its government can defend. In 1992, Britain spent billions defending the pound for one day. Then it lost. Why?

September 16th, 1992. By 9 a.m., the Bank of England had already spent more than a billion pounds buying back its own currency. At 11, it raised interest rates from 10 to 12 percent. At 2:15, it promised 15. In the money markets, overnight cash was quoted at 100 percent.
None of it worked. By about 7:30 that evening, it was over. In a few hours, Britain had thrown more than 22 billion dollars at the market... and lost.
[panicking] A hundred percent? For one night?
[smug, deep, rich] Pricier than a hotel in peak season.
On the other side of that trade sat one fund, run out of New York, holding a bet of about ten billion dollars that Britain would break its own promise. It walked away with about a billion.
So how does one fund beat a whole country? To answer that, we need to go back to a promise Britain made two years earlier.

Imagine your rupee, your pound or your dollar changed value against its neighbours every single day. For a factory selling across Europe in the 1980s, that was normal. Profits could vanish because a currency wobbled overnight.

So in 1979, a group of European countries built a fence. It was called the Exchange Rate Mechanism, or ERM. Each currency could drift, but only inside a band. Hit the edge of the band, and the central bank had to step in and defend it.

Britain stayed out for over a decade. Then, on October 8th, 1990, it jumped in. The rate: one pound for 2.95 Deutschmarks. The band: six percent either way. The floor: 2.778. Below that, the Bank of England had to buy pounds, whatever it cost. The man who signed Britain up was the finance minister, Chancellor John Major. The same day, rates were cut from 15 to 14 percent.

Why tie yourself to Germany? Because Britain had a price problem. In 1990, inflation hit 10.9 percent. Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, was the toughest inflation fighter in the world. Peg your money to the Deutschmark, and you borrow its reputation.
It's like a student who can't stop spending, handing his card to the strictest friend he has. It works... as long as the friend's plans match yours.

lines: Here's the catch. Days before Britain joined, East and West Germany reunited. Rebuilding the East cost enormous sums, and German money started growing too fast. By July 1992, German money supply was running around 9 percent against a target of 3.5 to 5.5.
So the Bundesbank did what it always did. It raised rates. The discount rate went to 8.75 percent. The Lombard rate sat at 9.75. For Germany, that made sense.

For Britain, it was a disaster. Britain was in a recession. Homeowners were drowning. Lenders repossessed about 75,000 homes in 1991, and nearly 69,000 more in 1992. By the end of 1992, somewhere between one and two million households owed more than their homes were worth.
And here's the cruel part. The peg was working. By the summer of 1992, British inflation was down to 3.6 percent. The medicine had done its job. But Britain couldn't stop taking it.

Britain needed cheaper money. But with the pound pinned near its floor, it couldn't cut rates without the pound sinking through it. Its interest rates were now set, in effect, by a central bank in Frankfurt, worrying about Berlin.
That's the mirage in this story. A fixed exchange rate looks like a fact. It isn't. It's a promise, and it only holds while someone is willing and able to defend it.
[sheepish] So the price on me is just... a promise?

Across the Atlantic, someone was watching that promise very closely. George Soros ran the Quantum Fund in New York. Day to day, it was managed by Stanley Druckenmiller, and by most accounts, the pound trade was his idea.

Here's how you bet against a currency. You borrow pounds, and immediately sell them for Deutschmarks at around 2.78. If the pound later falls to, say, 2.50, you buy those pounds back cheaper, return what you borrowed, and keep the difference.

Now look at the odds. The pound was sitting near its floor. If Britain held the line, the pound could only rise a little, so the bet loses a little. If Britain broke, the pound could fall a long way, and the bet wins big.
Heads, you lose a little. Tails, you win a lot. Traders dream of a bet like that.

But wait. Isn't the Bank of England unbeatable? It can print as many pounds as it likes. Here's the problem. To hold up the pound, it has to buy pounds, and pay for them in other currencies, like Deutschmarks and dollars. Those come from its reserves. And the Bank of England can't print a single Deutschmark. Its pockets are deep. But they have a bottom.

And Soros had a hunch about Germany. Economic historian Alain Naef found that Soros met Bundesbank president Helmut Schlesinger in Basel, and came away convinced the lira and the pound would soon fall. Germany, he reckoned, would not bend to save them.
[delighted] Ooh, a man who reads the room.

lines: By late summer 1992, the cracks were showing. John Major was now Prime Minister. In August, his new Chancellor, Norman Lamont, said Britain would do whatever is necessary to stay in. On September 3rd, the government announced it would borrow 10 billion ECU, Europe's accounting currency, about 7 billion pounds, to defend sterling.
Then Italy blinked. Over the weekend of September 12th, the lira was devalued by 7 percent. In return, Germany trimmed its rates. Just slightly. Less than markets hoped.

Then came the spark. On Tuesday, September 15th, after the London markets closed, Schlesinger spoke to reporters from Handelsblatt and the Wall Street Journal. In substance: the weekend's deal should have been broader, and more pressure on currencies couldn't be ruled out.

By that evening, it was on the news wires. Traders read it one way: the pound is next. That day, the Bank of England had already sold about 788 million dollars to prop up the pound. It closed at 2.7812. Barely above the floor.

Druckenmiller wanted to add to the bet. According to Druckenmiller himself, and financial historian Sebastian Mallaby, Soros told him to go for the jugular. They didn't just bet the fund. They bet roughly twice the fund. By Soros's own estimate, the position was worth almost ten billion dollars.

Before we get to Wednesday morning: every money trick in this story worked because people didn't look closely. Looking closely is the whole point of Money Mirage. If that's your thing, subscribe. Now... 8 a.m.

lines: Wednesday, September 16th, 1992. By 8 a.m., the pound is at 2.7794 Deutschmarks. That's a hair above the floor. The Bank of England starts buying. By 9, it has spent more than a billion pounds. The pound doesn't move. Help from Germany? According to Naef, the Bundesbank bought pounds for Britain just once that day: about 809 million pounds.
At 11 a.m., the big gun. Interest rates go from 10 to 12 percent in one move. The idea: make holding pounds so rewarding that sellers stop selling. They keep selling.
Lamont later said that once the rate rise failed, he told Prime Minister John Major the game was up. But Britain wasn't done.

At 2:15 p.m., it announces rates will rise again, to 15 percent. Fifteen. For a country already in recession. Overnight cash in the money markets is quoted at 100 percent. Everyone can see what's happening. A government raising rates this fast isn't strong. It's desperate.
[calmly sipping] I'd sell you too, darling.

Around 4 p.m., the Bank of England tells other central banks Britain is leaving. And at about 7:30 p.m., Lamont walks out into the Treasury courtyard, and announces that the pound is suspended from the ERM.

The 15 percent hike is cancelled that night. The next morning, rates are back to 10. In a few hours, Britain had sold more than 22 billion dollars of its reserves trying to hold a price the market no longer believed.

lines: Freed from its floor, the pound fell. By the end of 1992, it was around 2.45 Deutschmarks, roughly 17 percent below the rate Britain had promised. Against the dollar, it slid from about 1.85 to about 1.52.
Soros and his fund made about a billion dollars. And a hedge-fund manager almost nobody outside finance had heard of got a new name: the man who broke the Bank of England.

And Britain? Spending reserves isn't the same as losing them. The real loss came from buying pounds at the old price, and watching them fall. When Treasury papers were finally released in 2005, the best estimate of the cost was 3.3 billion pounds. About 57 pounds for every man, woman and child in the country.
[deadpan] No. You were the fifty-seven pounds.

The political bill was bigger. Just before the crisis, the governing Conservatives were level with Labour in one poll, at 38 each. By late November, Gallup had them at 29, against Labour's 52. In 1997, Labour won by a majority of 178 seats.

Britain wasn't alone, either. Major later told Parliament that no system could have survived an attack on that scale. In Sweden, he said, overnight rates had hit around 500 percent. Across that crisis, the Bundesbank alone was forced to spend about 65 billion Deutschmarks propping up other people's currencies.

A few days after the crash, in Washington, Lamont joked that his wife had heard him singing in the bath. He later said he was misreported. The voters weren't singing. By May 1993, Lamont was out of the Treasury.

lines: Now the twist. Without the peg, Britain could finally set its own rates. By November, they were down to 7 percent. In October 1992, it adopted something new: an inflation target, a public goal of 1 to 4 percent. And on May 6th, 1997, just days after winning power, Labour's new Chancellor, Gordon Brown, gave the Bank of England the power to set rates itself. Lamont says Brown phoned him the day before, to say Labour was taking his advice.
Many economists credit the cheaper pound and that new target with the recovery that followed. And Britain never joined the euro.
So was Soros the villain? He didn't create Britain's problem. He spotted it. A country had promised a price it couldn't afford to keep, and he bet that the promise would break before the bank did.

That's the lesson, and it's bigger than 1992. Whenever someone promises you a fixed price while the market quietly disagrees, a currency peg, a guaranteed return, a coin that's always worth one dollar, ask one question. Who's defending it, and how deep are their pockets?
[quietly] So every promise has a price tag.
A promise is only as strong as what stands behind it. When that runs out, the mirage disappears.

Money is full of promises like this one: prices, pegs and deals that aren't what they seem. Seeing through them is what this channel is for. Subscribe to Money Mirage, and next time, we'll break another one.
